idiom_name: symantic as a duck-typed object (sym.int / sym.add), interpreter injected at call time
implementation_notes: Ruby dispenses with the type-class layer entirely: any object that responds to the algebra's methods is an interpreter, and the program is a method taking it (`def exp(sym) = ...`), so the same expression is evaluated, printed or recorded by passing a different object. What replaces the classic structure: a parameter plus Ruby's message dispatch (`respond_to?`, and `method_missing` if a generated interpreter is wanted); `Dry::Monads` supplies Result/Option monads and do-notation for programs whose effect is itself a monad, but it is a monad library, not a higher-kinded layer, so effect polymorphism stays a convention. Justified for testable boundaries in ordinary Ruby; there is nothing to gain from adding type-level machinery to a language without static types.
code_sketch:
def exp(sym)                       # the program: only the algebra is named
  sym.add(sym.int(1), sym.add(sym.int(2), sym.int(4)))
end

eval_sym = Object.new
def eval_sym.int(i) = i
def eval_sym.add(a, b) = a + b

pretty_sym = Object.new
def pretty_sym.int(i) = i.to_s
def pretty_sym.add(a, b) = "(#{a} + #{b})"

exp(eval_sym)      # => 7        exp(pretty_sym) # => "(1 + (2 + 4))"
pitfalls: No compile-time contract: a missing operation raises NoMethodError only when that branch is reached, so interpreter completeness has to be asserted by tests (`respond_to?` checks or a shared conformance spec).
Singleton methods (`def obj.int`) are the idiom but cannot be marshalled or `dup`-ed - define the interpreter as a class when it must survive serialisation or copying.
Injecting an interpreter by reopening `Object`/`Kernel` (a common shortcut) leaks the meaning into every other spec in the process; keep the dictionary a parameter.
Keyword versus positional arguments drift silently between program and interpreters, and a shared mutable interpreter accumulates state across examples.
